## How an issue-title edit becomes searchable, and how a search query is served

**The write path (editing the title).** A title edit enters through the Server Action `updateIssueAction` in `src/actions/issues/update-issue.ts`, which is wrapped by `withAction` (`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts`). `withAction` first validates the payload with `updateIssueSchema` (`src/schemas/issue.ts`) — `title` must be a string between 3 and 200 characters if present — and resolves the acting user into an `Actor` via `resolveActorFor`/`getSessionPrincipal` (`src/lib/actor.ts`, `src/lib/session.ts`). The action handler then does a coarse `can(actor, "issue:update", …)` pre-check (`src/lib/permissions.ts`) before calling the real work in `updateIssue()` in `src/server/services/issue-service.ts`. That service function enforces tenant scoping with `assertOrgScope` (`src/lib/tenant.ts`), loads the current row with `issueRepo.findIssueById`, re-checks permission authoritatively against the real `authorId`/`assigneeId` via `assertCan`, refuses edits to archived issues via `assertNotArchived` (`src/lib/soft-delete.ts`), and finally writes the new title with `issueRepo.updateIssue()` in `src/server/repositories/issue-repository.ts`.

**Keeping the search copy in sync.** There's no database trigger and no external search engine — synchronization is done with an in-process event bus. After the write succeeds, `updateIssue()` calls `emit("issue.updated", { orgId, issueId, projectId, changedFields })` (`src/lib/event-bus.ts`). At startup, `registerSearchListeners()` in `src/server/services/search-service.ts` has subscribed to that event (alongside `issue.created`, `issue.archived`, comment/project events, and a manual reindex event). Its handler deliberately ignores the event payload's field values and re-reads the issue row fresh via `issueRepo.findIssueById(orgId, issueId)`, then calls `indexIssue(orgId, issue)`, which concatenates `title + "\n" + (description ?? "")` into a single `content` string and calls `searchRepo.upsertSearchDocument(orgId, "issue", issue.id, content, projectId)` (`src/server/repositories/search-repository.ts`). That upsert keys on `(orgId, subjectKind, subjectId)`, so the same search-index row is updated in place rather than duplicated. Because `emit()` awaits subscribers via `Promise.allSettled` and swallows failures, indexing normally completes before the action returns (so the colleague's search "moments later" typically just works), but a failure in the indexer never fails or blocks the original title edit — meaning the index *can* silently drift, which is why a separate batch job, `runSearchReindexJob` in `src/server/jobs/search-reindex-job.ts`, exists to walk and re-index everything in an org on demand.

**What's stored in the search copy.** The `search_index` table (`src/server/db/schema/webhooks.ts`) holds `id`, `orgId`, `subjectKind` (`"issue" | "comment" | "project"`), `subjectId`, an optional denormalized `projectId`, a single denormalized `content` text blob, and `indexedAt`. There is no tokenizer or FTS index — for an issue, `content` is just `title` followed by `description`; the "title" shown in results is reconstructed at query time as `content.split("\n")[0]`.

**The query path.** Two entry points converge on the same service: the Server Action `searchAction` (`src/actions/search/search.ts`) for the in-app search UI, and the route handler `GET /api/search` (`src/app/api/search/route.ts`) for the command palette. Both validate the request against `searchQuerySchema` (`src/schemas/search.ts`) — `q` must be 1–200 characters, `limit` 1–100, `kinds` a known enum — resolve the actor, and check `can(actor, "org:read", …)`, throwing/returning a permission error if denied. Both then call the shared `search()` function in `src/server/services/search-service.ts`, which re-checks tenant scope (`assertOrgScope`) and permission (`assertCan(actor, "issue:read", …)`) as defense in depth, then calls `consumeRateLimit(orgId, "search:query")` (`src/lib/rate-limit.ts`), a token bucket scaled by the org's plan. Finally it evaluates the `advanced_search` feature flag and, notably, checks `input.q.includes(":")` — if the query uses field-scoped syntax like `status:done` but the org's plan doesn't include `advanced_search`, the query is rejected outright with `"Field-scoped search is not included in this plan"` even though it's syntactically well-formed. Only after all of that does `searchRepo.searchDocuments()` run, filtering by `orgPredicate(orgId)` for tenant isolation, an optional `kinds`/`projectId` filter, a plain SQL `LIKE '%q%'` substring match on `content`, and keyset pagination ordered by `indexedAt`/`id`.

**Where a valid-looking query gets refused.** Beyond schema validation, a well-formed query can still be rejected for reasons unrelated to its shape: no session/no active org (`UnauthorizedActionError`); the requested `orgId` not matching the actor's own org (`TenantScopeError` / cross-tenant denial inside `can`/`explain`); insufficient role for `org:read`/`issue:read` (`ForbiddenActionError`/`PermissionDeniedError`); the `command_palette` feature flag being off (API route only); the org's token-bucket rate limit for `search:query` being exhausted; and — most subtly — using `:` field-scoped syntax without the `advanced_search` plan flag, which the service treats as a hard rejection rather than falling back to literal-text matching.
